I mostly enjoyed it, I thought there was a lot to like, quite a few great moments. My problems with it were that it never delves deep into any character, we only get to know everyone superficially and so while I was hooked by the visual and musical spectacle, I never felt full.

It's also rather pretentious I have to say, trying to do what *Casino* did for Las Vegas but for Hollywood, while also trying to pull some Space Odyssey existential trip, towards the end (of a very long movie) it all got to be too much.
It has been compared with Boogie Nights.

I hated this movie.

I mean its visually good, and I think the Pitt-Cava Storyline practically is a "great" film in my eyes. BUT I think Robbie's Nellie is just felt so empty yet full of explosive non-sense. This even extends with some of the minor characters (ie Lady Fay and that cabaret sequence). It feels like a suburban kid writes a fantasy storyline about those nitty gritty "gold-rush" of the Silent Era where everyone with a dream can be a star. It like watchin a Disney Channel view of what is shocking AND in fact, he practically just re-wrote the salacious rumors of famous Silent stars AND put it in the film.  Also, Nellie severely underwritten. It just gives you a reason to feel sad for Nellie but does not really want to color what kind of person she is. She just is freaky for freak sake. It just lacks a point of view on her part.  This is also half because Robbie just does not have the range too, which became a lose-lose situation. 

This has real potential to be honest BUT I think Chazelle just do not have a feminine viewpoint. He should get a co-writer because I somewhat felt this when I was watching La-la Land. Visually well done film but some characters feels un-drawn. Something human is missing about them.

I can see why many people had problems with this film. 

It tries hard to be like One Upon a Time in Hollywood and The Wolf of Wall Street, but it just doesn't work in the same way as either of those films at all.  

It felt like a movie for Hollywood elites to pat themselves on the back about. I think that's why it fundamentally doesn't work as well as it should've. 

Plus, this movie suffered from bad marketing and being released at a bad time as well.

I enjoyed parts of it, but at times was a bit bored. I kept thinking this must have cost a fortune to make, but doesn't really seem to be able to justify it. Overall, it's worth a watch, but left me feeling it could have been better.

As someone who watches a lot of silent movies, I was pretty frustrated with Chazelle's take on them, because it's clear he doesn't care about them at all, except as a cash engine that powered all the debauchery he's really interested in. For him the cinema that this world spawns all comes later, as we see by the montage at the end. He has no interest in the artistry that was actually happening at the time, except as passing references to party attendees.
It steals parts of Boogie Nights whole cloth.

It starts with an elephant shooting diarrhea in a dude's face 5 minutes in and ends up in Tobey Maguire's weird fight club thing.

I absolutely loved the big party sequence at the beginning, the big sequence where they're shooting like 3 silent films in the same place at the same time and the scene where they're shooting the first "talkie", the relationship between Margot Robbie and Diego Calva is pretty great imo and it's got some great dialogue here and there, but it also does some wild things that people who generally love movies about "the magic of cinema" don't like in their movies.

And then it throws Avatar in your face right in the end, lmao.

Chazelle clearly read the first 50 or so pages of Kevin Brownlow’s The Parade’s Gone By…, the definitive silent era nonfiction book, along with Kenneth Anger’s Hollywood Babylon. The era was truly as wild as he portrayed, and as unregulated, dirty, and dangerous. He then tossed Singin’ in the Rain, Boogie Nights, and The Wolf of Wall Street into the mix.

But I agree, by 1927, the industry was pretty mature, and audiences more sophisticated, than how it’s portrayed in the film.
I didn’t get the vibe of Hollywood elites patting themselves on the back at all. It’s a pretty unflattering portrayal of the industry.

Derivative, flat, nonsensical, tries to be both Baz Luhrmann and PT Anderson but feels like it's constantly contradicting itself. So many hat-on-a-hat-on-a-hat moments. All the poop jokes and its approach to sex made it feel like it was written by a 12-year-old. Excuse my Family Guy reference but I can't think of a movie that "insists upon itself" more.

I think Babylon is the sort of experiment one can get away with if the entire gamble wasn’t relying on an 80 million+ budget. Chazelle is a gifted director, but his qualities as a filmmaker were always mostly visual – even Whiplash, which was a banger and put him on the map, had a very thin script in terms of plot and character-depth; its impact was built by the incredible acting and scene staging and a killer sound design and editing. I get the feeling that he became more and more driven for peer approval after La La Land. The First Man was 'distinctive' enough to not come across as a basic biopic, but it also valued visuals over character-arc. Babylon was too indulgent and misguided.

I have to say I hated literally every minute of this film. The script is utterly ludicrous without a single believable moment or instant of subtlety. The characters are comic strip versions of human being distilled to one ridiculous essence and then heightened to absurdity. The performances are uniformly terrible. There is no plot to speak of. The technical elements and VFX are amateurish. The cinematography is badly-lit and extremely uneven and then editing is film school bad. 

So, yeah. A garbage fire start to finish.

Seriously, what exactly makes a plot thin? And I don't equate simple with thin. Look at Scorsese's Mean Streets. Brilliant film. But a simple plot. One guy trying to keep his friend out of trouble while dealing with his own morality. Was there character-depth or was it due to great acting by DeNiro, Keitel, Romano, etc.? difference is Mean Streets takes place in a timeframe of a few days whilst Babylon takes across approximately two decades.

I don’t know why, but I just don’t trust Chazelle’s vision as a director. 

I never believe his worlds. 

I never buy the emotional beats. 

He always has a good cast, he always has art direction and flashy editing. There’s clearly skill. And even though I don’t see the magic, other people do. 

I think what he ultimately lacks is an interesting voice. He has nothing to say other than, “I’m a fan of movies from this era” or “I love jazz from this era” or “i will do anything to be apart of the movies,  that I’m a fan of”.  

There is something interesting in the way that he views the act of art making. That one must transcend physical suffering to be great or sacrifice something to achieve a Hollywood dream. 

It’s just that I don’t think he has actually felt anything close to that, and he doesn’t know how to depict emotions other than through extremity that it ends up feeling empty or cliche. 

Chazelle still feels like he is in the stage of his career where he is trying to figure out his voice. What he actually wants to say. Underdeveloped is maybe what I’m getting at. 


If he didn’t have so many accolades, I think I wouldn’t have such high expectations. 

Also, like…. Unless you can pull it off, it’s a HUGE RISK to continue to reference and show clips of other films that are arguably more well known and beloved by generations of film goers. 

For you it was earnest, but for others it’s… questionable. 

I personally think, if you want to celebrate the magic of cinema, make your own magic.

I'm a working professional DP. 

Badly-lit because the lighting is irrational and unmotivated. The key often flips in a noticeable and distracting way from shot to shot during dialogue. And there are a lot of scenes where characters have two or three shadows. In a major motion picture that's a no- no.

Unevenly lit because it often jumps between hard light and soft light within the same scene, sometimes from shot to shot. Obviously, they were trying to emulate some old Hollywood lighting styles, but there's no rhyme or reason to it. Also, lighting that works in black & white often looks spectacularly bad in color. *Babylon* is the proof.

I am not sure if it was hated but more it was simply flop in cinemas. What isn't really surprising because there were made some decisions during productions which made film hard to marketing. I actually felt that their pr team simply gave up lol because film was tragically advertised lol

it might be because Whiplash has such a familiar middle-class setting and makes its dilemma so plain (cost of genius), it always feels safe compared to Mean Streets
Yeah I find it clear to see that it's a love it or hate it film.

So partway through watching I say to my wife "this is beat for beat Boogie Nights". Except it's made by someone why watched Boogie Nights and said "what if I remade it but removed all the character work?", so by the end you don't care about a single person.

 In Boogie Nights you see Whalbergs gradual fall into drug addiction. It's weaved into the movie. In Babylon, someone just says half way through the movie to Margo Robbie that she has to get her gambling problem under control. It's so random, there's been no setup. Nothing we've seen in the 120 minutes prior to that builds up her fall. It's just "gosh, she's great. *Insert scene from Singing in the Rain*. Oh, she gambles I guess?". It's like that for every character. Maybe Pitt is the only one with a little bit of a story that's properly dramatized? 

Anyway, just self indulgent without bothering to make me care about a single character. A worse copy of better movies.

Where *Boogie Nights* is very indebted to what Scorsese was doing with *Goodfellas* and *Casino*. But yeah, I do think *Boogie* is the more direct comp in terms of the “whacky” side of *Babylon’s* tone and the tracking of a type of film industry over the years. 

It’s an interesting comparison. *Boogie* has such a consistent tone. And for all its episodic nature, the arc of rise and fall is well drawn and paced. *Babylon* loses the plot in comparison, and tries to juggle too many balls. It feels flat footed when it tries to show how things got *so* dark and *gritty*, *man* (I’m sorry but the whole Tobey sequence could be dropped for my money), and by the thread about the transcendence of cinema. I don’t know, maybe that ending would have worked for me if it capped a different movie.
How is it "clear", again?

I wanted to add a note about David Lynch. Maybe it’s a false equivalent but Lynch also makes movies about the horrors and allure of Hollywood. They also depict extreme emotions and outlandish performances. He also references a tonne of films he loves and evokes past eras. 

The difference is (apart from the amount of experience) Lynch makes thoughtful choices that add depth and texture to his films. His interest in certain eras of cinema are rooted in personal experiences and actually living through the 50s.

When he references Gilda, it’s purposeful. You can draw a bunch of meanings from that idea. I don’t know what Singing in the Rain (aside from historical relevance) and Avatar add to the meaning of his film other than they are both Hollywood movies that can engender wonder. 

I don’t know what Rebel Without A Cause adds to a story about a creative couple struggling with work-life balance, other than it was also filmed in CinemaScope and shot in LA. 

I don’t know why he makes those choices besides thier function. He misses opportunities to build on the ideas in his movies.

I guess I wanted to add that there are examples of other filmmakers that tread similar territory in more refined ways.

Yeah, it's not a big deal to use Boogie Nights as a template, but you have to care about the character. Notice that nobody talks about the main character, because there's nothing interesting about him. 

These are my thoughts after watching it: 

> Chazelle knows how to construct a great scene, but he can't string those scenes into a story. The script is so fractured that it is less episodic and more an anthology of shorts. Of course, with any anthology, there are stories you like more than others, and I wish Chazelle had trimmed a few stories or characters to get the three hour runtime down to something bearable (I checked when I got bored and was shocked to see I was only halfway through). Even in those three hours, there are big chunks of character development that happen off screen (like Nellie's gambling) so you still feel like you're missing a bunch. La La Land had the exact same problem, but this time Chazelle is going overboard with ambition and Baz Luhrmannesque excess, and there are a lot of nice moments throughout. One thing is for sure, he really loves movies, although ending with a film that tells your story much better than you did may not have been a great choice.

Agreed that it's fine to use Boogie Nights, I mean, that movie is essentialy "porn Goodfellas" anyway, so it's not original either. The difference is PTA actually cared about the characters, while Chazelle just didn't. At all.

I share a lot of your reactions but think it's even worse. Not only was Nelly severely underwritten but so was the trumpet player whose career was cut short because the studios wanted to pander to racist audiences. His role and place in the story arc was so thin and perfunctory that even the movie's superfans don't mention it in their under-thought, half-baked fist-pumping. 

The pivotal Jean Smart monologue to Brad Pitt about living on forever in celluloid is obvious nonsense when the era famously treated its own work as literally disposable and showed no interest in preserving films for posterity. I don't care if movies aren't faithful to history but this specific attempt to wring out depth or emotion felt especially pandering and cynical given that film preservation was not a concept at the time.

The elephant shit, the vomiting sequence, the nod to the (very false) Fatty Arbuckle legend, the Boogie Nights rip-off sequence with Tobey Maguire are all pathetic, adolescent, dumb, awkward.

The movie is a sloppy, try-hard mess from elephant-feces start to misty-eyed-Hollywood-montage finish. It's one of the biggest wastes of talent in the last twenty years.

>There is something interesting in the way that he views the act of art making. That one must transcend physical suffering to be great or sacrifice something to achieve a Hollywood dream (even though I think this is dated perspective and only runs surface deep). 

I don't think its surface cause of its self-consciousness. His films are more of character studies than we think of them as. They're about these very specific, overly-ambitious individuals whose attitudes differ from the rest of the world—they are somehow self-destructive, become alienated from their sorrounding and from their relationships. In Babylon you've got a mexican who cuts relationship with his family to follow a dream, an actor who achieved success (in every Chazelle film, "success" is in doubt) yet doesn't know what love is, a star who's afraid of relationships cause she fears she'll end uo hurting everyone around her, so she rather fade out as she does in the end... they are deeply painful films, and what are these characters looking for? Perhaps it isn't even about the movies, as Whiplash is less about jazz and more about a kid who seeks for validation.

>I don’t know why he makes those choices outside of thier function. He misses opportunities to build on the ideas in his movies.

Yeah, it's interesting because Chazelle doesn't make much of a relecture of the films he's making references to. Reminds me of this year's The Substance's short reference to Vertigo, which felt empty and more of whim rather than a thoughtful inclusion.

La La Land is a bit of a whim itself... it's drowned in a self-defeating nostalgia that both enchants you with it's references while at the same time making you go "Astaire and Rogers danced better than Gosling and Stone do...", it's a bit of it's charm, I think it fits. Babylon can be a bit more irritating, though.

I liked Babylon a lot, but it was probably doomed to fail from the beginning.  

It was too artsy for mainstream audiences, but the major Hollywood stars and wide theatrical release probably scared off the arthouse crowd.

It has elements of a musical, and the musical genre is highly divisive.  You either love musicals or you hate them. Personally, I despise musicals.  

It was a long movie and mainstream audiences don't care about the silent film era.  

Also, the "love letter to cinema" thing has been done a million times before and isn't particularly original.  

All that said, I think this is one of those movies that will eventually be recognized as a great film.

The reason I say “surface deep” is because of how those characters and their choices are depicted through visual story telling.

It’s his choices as a director that I don’t trust because I always think there is another more thoughtful way of finding a character beat. I think he makes obvious choices. And I think if he got to spend more time making smaller films he could exercise that muscle.

If that’s his voice, fine. If that’s his vision, cool. He just doesn’t sell me the emotional lives of these characters, whoever they are. 

Maybe for Babylon, people can’t connect with those character motivations because in La La land and Whiplash there was a singular dynamic to engage with. People don’t have to love musicals or jazz to be obsessed with those stories. 

Maybe in Babylon, audiences don’t have a chance to fall in love with the film because there isn’t one singular dynamic to hook them in so the “study” is a little spread out and unfocused.
Tbh I’ve trying to be kind to these films in these replies. I’m a bit of a grumpy guts when it comes to La La land 😅

There's definitely some interesting things about the film, it's just all over the place. 

* For a 3 hour movie, the characters and connections feel thin.
* There are some great set pieces, but then it's filled with things like the snake scene. The gangster/Nellie section really dragged. 
* The movie tried to have it both ways. It shows the ugly side of Hollywood. Most of the characters are in it for the fame, sex, drugs, power moves, and excess, plus racism and homophobia. But then it's also supposed to be about the magic of movies. There should have been more scenes with Manny falling in love with the craft so that the ending feels earned. 

I actually didn't hate the movie. I thought it was worth watching - the score is stunning, the cast is shot gorgeously, and I loved Robbie. But it just was disappointing because I feel there was a great movie in there somewhere.

>The script is utterly ludicrous without a single believable moment or instant of subtlety. The characters are comic strip versions of human beings distilled to one ridiculous essence and then heightened to absurdity.

Isn't that the point? These characters being stripped out of any inch of humanity is on par with the idea of a "machine" stripping human beings alive to make them fit into a system; reduced to spectacle and stereotypes, their true self are lost to the audience. It is a very cynical view on Hollywood and art, especially on acting—actors are shown as victims, abused and deceived. In fact, Hollywood is shown as this dehumanizing place where artists have to inflict pain on each other in order to power climb within the industry they're in/want to become part of (already a theme in the director's other work, La La Land). And so, the film is this weird shit where characters go from being seemingly one-dimensional, paper-thin cariactures (goes perfectly for the satire elements in the film) to bursting into attemps of being human once again, even if it's too late... (I can think of a scene or two where this happens).

I believe it's much more subtle than many people gave it a chance to be, you have to read deeper into the soul of the piece itself, which is as deformed as you describe it to be, bended by it's heavy cynicism and self-loathing but with inches of love and hope seeping in its final moments: "I don't think I'm very good for you."

You might be right but, I'll be honest, for me, the view will never be worth the climb.The film is so *technically* awful, I had a really difficult time sitting through it once. Mercifully, I was at home where I could shout at the screen. But I'll never watch it again, and certainly won't be investing in a deep dive to find the value in a movie I found valueless. 

Even if you're correct, the film still has to be endurable and interesting to tell that story, and I would argue it fails on both points. Loud Reed's "Metal Machine" *might* be a brilliant work of post-pop allegory, but I'll never listen through it to find out because it's painful to listen to.

Story first, always. *Babylon* has none.
